content: 1. There is no FDA guidance regarding the use of Losartan in specific gender populations. 2. There is no FDA guidance on the use of Losartan in specific racial populations. 3. There is no FDA guidance on the use of Losartan in patients with renal impairment. 4. There is no FDA guidance on the use of Losartan in patients with hepatic impairment. 5. There is no FDA guidance on the use of Losartan in women of reproductive potential or in males. 6. There is no FDA guidance on the use of Losartan in immunocompromised patients. 7. Losartan is administered orally. 8. The FDA package insert for Losartan does not provide information regarding drug monitoring. 9. There is limited information available about the intravenous (IV) compatibility of Losartan. 10. Significant lethality was observed in mice and rats after oral administration of 1000 mg/kg and 2000 mg/kg, respectively, which corresponds to approximately 44 and 170 times the maximum recommended human dose on a mg/m² basis. 11. Limited data are available regarding Losartan overdose in humans. 12. The most likely manifestations of Losartan overdose are hypotension and tachycardia, although bradycardia may occur due to parasympathetic (vagal) stimulation. 13. If symptomatic hypotension occurs, supportive treatment should be initiated. 14. Neither Losartan nor its active metabolite can be removed by hemodialysis. 15. Angiotensin II is a potent vasoconstrictor and the primary vasoactive hormone of the renin-angiotensin system, playing a key role in the pathophysiology of hypertension. 16. Angiotensin II also stimulates aldosterone secretion by the adrenal cortex. 17. Losartan and its principal active metabolite block the vasoconstrictor and aldosterone-secreting effects of Angiotensin II by selectively inhibiting its binding to the AT1 receptor, which is found in various tissues such as vascular smooth muscle and the adrenal gland. 18. The AT2 receptor, also found in many tissues, is not known to be associated with cardiovascular homeostasis. 19. Neither Losartan nor its active metabolite exhibits partial agonist activity at the AT1 receptor, and both have a much greater affinity (approximately 1000-fold) for the AT1 receptor compared to the AT2 receptor. 20. In vitro binding studies indicate that Losartan is a reversible, competitive inhibitor of the AT1 receptor. 21. The active metabolite of Losartan is 10 to 40 times more potent by weight than Losartan itself and appears to act as a reversible, non-competitive inhibitor of the AT1 receptor. 22. Neither Losartan nor its active metabolite inhibits ACE (kininase II, the enzyme that converts Angiotensin I to Angiotensin II and degrades bradykinin), nor do they bind to or block other hormone receptors or ion channels involved in cardiovascular regulation. 23. Losartan potassium is an angiotensin II receptor (type AT1) antagonist. 24. Chemically, Losartan potassium is described as 2-butyl-4-chloro-1-imidazole-5-methanol monopotassium salt, with an empirical formula of C22H22ClKN6O and a molecular weight of 461. 25. Losartan potassium is a white to off-white free-flowing crystalline powder that is freely soluble in water, soluble in alcohols, and slightly soluble in common organic solvents such as acetonitrile and methyl ethyl ketone. 26. Oxidation of the 5-hydroxymethyl group on the imidazole ring results in the active metabolite of Losartan. 27. Losartan inhibits the pressor effects of Angiotensin II (and Angiotensin I) infusions. 28. A 100 mg dose of Losartan inhibits the pressor effect by approximately 85% at peak, with 25-40% inhibition persisting for 24 hours. 29. Removal of the negative feedback of Angiotensin II causes a 2to 3-fold increase in plasma renin activity and a consequent rise in Angiotensin II plasma concentration in hypertensive patients. 30. Losartan does not affect the response to bradykinin, whereas ACE inhibitors enhance the response to bradykinin. 31. Plasma aldosterone concentrations decrease following Losartan administration. 32. Despite its effect on aldosterone secretion, Losartan has minimal impact on serum potassium levels. 33. In a single-dose study in normal volunteers, Losartan had no effects on glomerular filtration rate, renal plasma flow, or filtration fraction. 34. In multiple-dose studies in hypertensive patients, Losartan showed no significant effects on systemic or renal prostaglandin concentrations, fasting triglycerides, total cholesterol, HDL-cholesterol, or fasting glucose concentrations. 35. A small uricosuric effect was observed, leading to a minimal decrease in serum uric acid (mean decrease <0.4 mg/dL) during chronic oral administration. 36. 37. 38. Twice-daily dosing at 50-100 mg/day provided consistently larger trough responses than once-daily dosing at the same total dose. 39. Peak (6-hour) effects were uniformly, but moderately, larger than trough effects, with trough-to-peak ratios for systolic and diastolic responses ranging from 50-95% and 60-90%, respectively. 40. Analysis of age, gender, and race subgroups showed that men and women, as well as patients over and under 65 years of age, had generally similar responses to Losartan. 42. 43. The antihypertensive effect of Losartan is substantially present within one week, but in some studies, the maximal effect occurred within 3-6 weeks. 44. In long-term follow-up studies (without placebo control), the effect of Losartan appeared to be maintained for up to a year. 45. There is no apparent rebound effect after abrupt withdrawal of Losartan. 46. There was essentially no change in average heart rate in Losartan-treated patients in controlled trials. 47. The antihypertensive effect of Losartan was studied in one trial involving 177 hypertensive pediatric patients aged 6 to 16 years. 48. Children weighing less than 50 kg received 2.5, 25, or 50 mg of Losartan daily, while those weighing 50 kg or more received 5, 50, or 100 mg daily. 49. Children in the lowest dose group were given Losartan in a suspension formulation. 50. The majority of the pediatric patients had hypertension associated with renal and urogenital disease.
